stories.headline: Army blows up unstable lead explosives in Iowa and reports no airborne lead
stories.summary: The Army detonated nearly five tons of degraded lead azide at its ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Wednesday after a federal court allowed the operation to go ahead. The Army and the EPA said monitors found no airborne lead afterward, and testing of air, soil and water continues. Scientists and residents told NBC News they still want to know how much contamination the blast left behind.
stories.why_it_matters: Lead dust is a health hazard, especially for children, and people in the area around the plant were told to evacuate or stay indoors. The test results in the coming days will show whether homes, soil and water nearby were affected.
stories.background: Lead azide is a highly sensitive explosive used in munitions, and it contains lead. The Army said a stockpile at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown had degraded and become unstable, and that destroying it where it sat was safer than moving it. The blast was first planned for Nov. 20 but was pushed back amid public health concerns and what CBS News described as days of back-and-forth between politicians and the courts. Authorities evacuated a five-mile radius, and federal officials told people within 20 miles who had not left to shelter in place.

facts.text: The Army detonated a degraded stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday.
The stockpile amounted to nearly five tons of material.
The Army and the EPA said emission monitors detected no airborne lead in the surrounding region immediately after the explosion, and the EPA said it will keep testing air, soil and water.
The detonation went ahead after a federal court allowed it; Army officials called the operation a success but did not take reporters' questions, PBS NewsHour reported.
Six federal agencies said in a joint statement that the shelter-in-place order for Middletown was lifted on Wednesday, according to The Hill.
Authorities evacuated a five-mile radius before the blast, and federal officials said people within 20 miles who had not evacuated should shelter in place.
Scientists and Iowa residents told NBC News that questions remain about how much contamination the blast caused, though they were hopeful about the first results.
Three states said they are monitoring the effects.
Vice President JD Vance defended the detonation while visiting troops at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio on Wednesday.

Before the blast, the Army said destroying about 10,000 pounds of degraded lead azide in place was the only responsible option because moving it risked an accidental explosion, and the EPA issued an emergency permit.

stories.headline: Trump proposes new tariffs of up to 20% on 14 trading partners; China warns it may retaliate
stories.summary: The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed new tariffs of up to 20 percent on goods from 14 trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union, after an investigation into what it calls excess industrial capacity abroad. China, the EU and others criticized the plan on Thursday while leaving the door open to talks, and China warned it could retaliate. Democrats who will control Congress next year are preparing to challenge the tariffs, the Washington Examiner reported.
stories.why_it_matters: Tariffs are taxes on imports, and businesses often pass them on, so the plan could raise prices on everyday goods. Retaliation by other countries could also hurt American exporters.
stories.background: President Trump has used tariffs throughout his second term, arguing they protect American companies and bring factory jobs back. In March the U.S. Trade Representative opened investigations into whether other economies subsidize their manufacturers into producing more than the market needs, a step Reuters described at the time as an effort to rebuild tariff pressure. Wednesday's proposal is the result of that investigation. It comes three weeks after midterm elections in which Republicans lost ground, and while a trade truce between Washington and Beijing is in place.

facts.text: The administration proposed new tariffs of up to 20 percent on 14 trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union.
The proposal follows a U.S. investigation into alleged global overcapacity and government subsidies for manufacturers.
China, the EU and other trading partners criticized the plan on Thursday while holding out the possibility of negotiations.
China warned it could retaliate if the duties go ahead, and The Wall Street Journal reported the tariffs could undermine the U.S.-China trade truce.
Bloomberg reported that the tariffs could weaken the incentive for companies to move production out of China, because other manufacturing countries are also targeted.
Incoming Democratic majorities in Congress are set to challenge Trump's tariffs, according to the Washington Examiner.
The U.S. Trade Representative opened the excess-capacity investigations in March 2026, covering 16 economies.

stories.headline: Judge blocks FCC's early review of ABC station licenses, citing free speech
stories.summary: U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan on Wednesday night issued a preliminary injunction barring the Federal Communications Commission from taking further action on an early review of broadcast licenses for Disney-owned ABC stations. The Washington Post reported she found the review probably violates the First Amendment. The order is temporary while the lawsuit continues.
stories.why_it_matters: The case tests whether a federal regulator can use broadcast licenses to pressure a network over what it airs, which affects what news and entertainment viewers get from local stations. In the day's feed the ruling was covered by left-leaning and center outlets but no right-leaning ones.
stories.background: The FCC licenses local TV stations and normally reviews them when they are due to expire; ABC's were not set to expire until 2028. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr ordered an early review earlier this year, a day after President Trump called on ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel, according to Deutsche Welle. Disney and ABC sued in August, arguing the review was meant to punish speech the administration dislikes. The FCC has argued that the court lacks jurisdiction over the dispute.

facts.text: Judge Loren AliKhan granted a preliminary injunction Wednesday night prohibiting the FCC from taking further action on its early renewal review of ABC's broadcast licenses.

ABC argued the review was an attempt by the Trump administration to punish speech it does not like and had a chilling effect on the network.
The FCC chairman ordered the early review a day after Trump called for ABC to fire Jimmy Kimmel, and the licenses were not due to expire until 2028, Deutsche Welle reported.

stories.headline: A second federal judge blocks Trump's new birthright citizenship order
stories.summary: U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper in Washington on Wednesday blocked enforcement of President Trump's second executive order limiting who gets citizenship at birth. Trump signed that order after the Supreme Court rejected his first attempt. Cooper is the second judge to rule against the new order.
stories.why_it_matters: The order would decide whether some babies born in the United States are citizens, which affects passports, benefits and the right to stay. In the day's feed the ruling was covered by center and right-leaning outlets but no left-leaning ones.
stories.background: The Fourteenth Amendment says people born in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction are citizens. Trump's first order restricting that for children of some immigrants was rejected by the Supreme Court. He then signed a narrower order, which a federal judge in Maryland blocked in early September, citing the Supreme Court's decision. Wednesday's ruling in Washington is the second against the new order.

stories.headline: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves the U.S. for Spain, ending a 20-month deportation fight
stories.summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran man the government mistakenly deported last year, left the United States voluntarily on Tuesday and landed in Madrid on Wednesday. A judge then closed his case, The Washington Times reported. His lawyer called the move temporary and said he hopes to return to his family in Maryland after President Trump leaves office.
stories.why_it_matters: His case became the best-known test of whether the government must give people a hearing before deporting them. It ends with him leaving and with no final court ruling on some of the questions it raised.
stories.background: Abrego Garcia, 31, lived in Maryland and was deported to El Salvador in March 2025 in what the government acknowledged was an error. He was brought back to the United States after a Supreme Court ruling, and the administration then sought to deport him again while also charging him with human smuggling. A federal judge dismissed those criminal charges in May. Homeland Security officials have continued to describe him as a gang member, and his case became a focal point in the debate over Trump's deportation policies.

stories.headline: Georgia judge pauses her own order to hand Fulton County's 2020 ballot copies to state board
stories.summary: Fulton County Superior Court Judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe on Tuesday ordered the county to give Georgia's State Election Board digital copies of 2020 ballots and other election records. On Wednesday she put that order on hold after county election officials objected in a court filing. The records stay with the county for now.
stories.why_it_matters: The 2020 results in Georgia have been counted and reviewed several times, and this fight is over who gets to examine the ballots again. The outcome could shape how much power the state board has over county election offices in future elections.
stories.background: Fulton County, which includes most of Atlanta, is Georgia's most populous county and has been the focus of President Trump's claims about the 2020 election. The State Election Board, which sets and enforces Georgia's election rules, has sought certain 2020 records from the county for more than two years. NBC News describes the board as controlled by allies of Trump. The FBI seized the county's 2020 ballots and related materials earlier this year, and a federal judge later ruled the Justice Department could keep them.

facts.text: On Tuesday a judge ordered Fulton County to turn over a digital copy of 2020 ballots and other election records to the State Election Board.
On Wednesday the judge, Kelly Lee Ellerbe of Fulton County Superior Court, paused her own order after county election officials made a filing in the case.
The records were among materials the FBI seized from the county earlier this year.
The State Election Board had been trying for more than two years to obtain certain 2020 records from the county.
Tuesday's order required unredacted digital copies of the election materials, NBC News reported.
Members of the State Election Board are split on the records case, The Center Square reported.

stories.headline: Fort Hood shooter asks federal court to delay next week's firing-squad execution
stories.summary: Nidal Hasan, the former Army major who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, moved in federal court on Tuesday to delay his execution by firing squad, which is scheduled for next week. stories.background: In November 2009 Hasan, then an Army major, opened fire at Fort Hood, a large Army post in Texas, killing 13 people and wounding more than 30. He was convicted of murder and attempted murder and sentenced to death. The Pentagon scheduled his execution by firing squad for early December. An initial proposal to livestream it drew public outrage, NBC News reported.

stories.headline: Trump and NATO chief tell Russia not to widen the Ukraine war
stories.summary: President Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte met at Mar-a-Lago on Wednesday and, in a joint statement released by the White House, urged Russia to avoid any actions that would expand the war in Ukraine and called for a quick peaceful settlement. The statement came as fighting reached beyond the two countries' borders: forces controlling eastern Libya threatened to retaliate against Ukraine over a drone strike on a Russian warship near Benghazi, and Poland said it plans a no-fly zone near its border with Ukraine.
stories.why_it_matters: The war is touching more countries, from Poland's border to the Mediterranean, which raises the risk of a wider conflict involving NATO members and of further shocks to energy prices.
stories.background: Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and the war is now in its fifth year. NATO, the US-led military alliance headed by Mark Rutte, backs Ukraine with weapons and money but is not fighting in the war. Ukraine has increasingly struck Russian oil facilities and ships far from the front line, while Russia has been hitting Ukraine's power system as winter begins. Libya is split between rival administrations, and the eastern one, led by the Libyan National Army, has close ties to Russia. Trump has pushed for a negotiated end to the war and met Russian President Vladimir Putin last week in Asia.

facts.text: Trump and Rutte urged Russia to avoid actions that would widen the war in Ukraine after meeting at Mar-a-Lago, in a joint statement released by the White House.
The joint statement described the meeting as "outstanding" and "very impactful."
The two also called for a rapid peaceful resolution, as Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure intensify, CNBC reported.
Trump met Putin last week in Asia and referred to him as a "friend," according to the Reuters report carried by the Japan Times.
The Libyan National Army said two of its soldiers died Tuesday in a Ukrainian drone strike on a Russian warship near Benghazi, and it vowed to retaliate.
Poland plans a no-fly zone near its border with Ukraine and has asked NATO to intercept Russian missiles over Ukraine, the Kyiv Independent reported.
Ukraine's General Staff confirmed strikes on two Russian oil refineries in Samara Oblast, the Kyiv Independent reported.
Some NATO countries have voiced growing concern about the war spreading to new regions as Ukraine attacks Russian ships in distant waters, CBS News reported.
In April, two Libyan officials told the Associated Press that Ukrainian forces operating from western Libya had struck a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean.

stories.headline: Fuel tanker fire on Cairo's ring road kills at least 31
stories.summary: A fuel tanker crash on the Ring Road around Cairo on Wednesday set off a fire that spread to nearby vehicles and killed at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said. The public prosecutor's office said a suspected driver was arrested on Thursday. Health authorities said the death toll could rise.

stories.background: The Ring Road is a major highway that circles greater Cairo, a metropolitan area of more than 20 million people, and it is usually packed with cars, minibuses and motorcycles. Egypt has a long record of deadly road crashes, often blamed on speeding, poorly maintained roads and loose enforcement of traffic rules. The crash happened in Giza, on the western side of the capital. Egypt's public prosecutor is leading the investigation.

stories.headline: Kim Jong Un tours nuclear material plants and calls for more tactical nuclear weapons
stories.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear material and said the country should deploy tactical nuclear weapons more widely, state news agency KCNA reported Thursday. He said production capacity for nuclear material is being expanded and that North Korea's status as a nuclear state will not change. The visit follows President Trump's renewed offer of talks, which Pyongyang has not taken up.
stories.why_it_matters: Tactical nuclear weapons are smaller arms meant for battlefield use against nearby targets such as South Korea and Japan, where tens of thousands of US troops are based. More of them makes a nuclear crisis in the region harder to manage.
stories.background: North Korea has tested nuclear weapons six times since 2006 and is under United Nations sanctions over its weapons programs. Trump met Kim three times in 2018 and 2019, but the talks collapsed without a deal on giving up the weapons. Since then Kim has declared the country's nuclear status permanent and expanded its missile and warhead programs. Almost everything known about visits like this one comes from KCNA, the state news agency, and cannot be independently checked.

stories.headline: Israeli judges suggest dropping most charges against Netanyahu; he demands the trial end
stories.summary: The judges hearing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial advised prosecutors on Wednesday to consider dropping most of the charges, including in the main bribery case. Netanyahu said the trial had "fallen apart" and must end immediately, and ministers in his government made the same demand. The judges' advice is not a verdict, and the decision on whether to withdraw charges rests with prosecutors.
stories.why_it_matters: The trial has shaped Israeli politics for years and decides whether a sitting prime minister can be convicted of corruption. How it ends will affect trust in Israel's courts and Netanyahu's political future.
stories.background: Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate cases, and his trial opened in 2020. The most serious case alleges he gave regulatory favors to a telecom owner in exchange for friendly news coverage. He denies all wrongdoing and calls the cases a political witch hunt. The trial has run alongside a bitter national fight over the power of the courts. The decision on whether to withdraw charges belongs to the state prosecution and the attorney general, not the judges.

stories.headline: EU leaders split over next budget and a new €45 billion loan for Ukraine
stories.summary: The European Union's 27 leaders met in Brussels on Thursday to negotiate the bloc's 2028-2034 budget and a proposed €45 billion loan to keep Ukraine funded through 2027. They disagreed over who should pay for the loan, with Germany pressing all members to contribute and some seeking exemptions. Several leaders said a budget deal was far off; talks were expected to run late and continue Friday.
stories.why_it_matters: The EU budget sets farm subsidies, regional aid and defense spending for 450 million people for seven years, and the loan helps decide whether Ukraine can keep paying for its defense and basic services next year.
stories.background: The EU agrees a long-term budget every seven years, and it needs the approval of all member governments, so talks usually drag on. Countries that pay in more than they get back, such as Germany and Denmark, want it kept smaller, while others defend farm and regional funds. Separately, the EU has become Ukraine's main financial backer; leaders agreed a €90 billion loan in December 2025 to cover much of 2026 and 2027. A summit in October ended without a budget deal.

Leaders were divided over who should pay for the Ukraine loan, Bloomberg reported.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said leaders remain "very far apart" and agreed with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz that the current budget proposal will not work, the Guardian reported.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said leaders were "light-years away" from a budget agreement, according to the Guardian.
France's main goal is to prevent cuts to Common Agricultural Policy subsidies, France 24 reported.
US tariffs and the choice of the next European Central Bank president are also on the agenda.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said Ukraine faces a winter "like hell" and must know Europe will back it financially.
EU leaders agreed in December 2025 on a €90 billion loan to cover much of Ukraine's financing needs for 2026 and 2027.

stories.headline: China puts Shanghai party chief Chen Jining under investigation
stories.summary: Chen Jining, the Communist Party secretary of Shanghai and a member of the 24-person Politburo, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of serious violations of party discipline and law, Chinese state media reported. He had been seen as a possible future national leader. Beijing is now weighing who will run the country's financial capital less than a year before a major party congress.
stories.why_it_matters: Shanghai is China's main financial hub, and the removal of one of the country's most senior officials shows how unsettled the top of the world's second-largest economy is before next year's leadership reshuffle.
stories.background: President Xi Jinping has run an anti-corruption campaign since taking power in 2012 that has removed large numbers of officials, including senior generals and party leaders. The Politburo is the party's top decision-making body, and the Shanghai post has often been a stepping stone to the very top. In China, an announcement that an official is under investigation for discipline violations almost always ends in removal and prosecution. The party holds its 21st congress in 2027, when top posts are reassigned.

facts.text: Chen Jining, Shanghai's party secretary and a Politburo member, was placed under investigation on suspicion of serious violations of discipline and law.
Chen had been seen as a potential future leader, the Wall Street Journal reported.
Chen is the fourth Politburo member brought down in the anti-corruption drive ahead of next year's leadership reshuffle, the South China Morning Post reported.
China's anti-corruption agency has detained 61 senior civilian officials so far this year, including two sitting Politburo members, according to a South China Morning Post tally.
The move breaks decades of precedent and leaves the Shanghai post open less than a year before the party's 21st congress, the South China Morning Post reported.

stories.background: Cartagena is a port city on Colombia's Caribbean coast and a major stop for cruise ships and foreign tourists. Colombia has struggled for decades with armed groups and organized crime, though this incident was described by the president as the work of ordinary criminals. stories.headline: 13 dead and 13 missing after flood in illegal Indonesian gold mine
stories.summary: Thirteen miners are confirmed dead and another 13 are missing after heavy rain flooded an unauthorized gold mine in Indonesia's West Java province on Monday, authorities said. Rescuers are working in high water, darkness and narrow passages, and continued rain is slowing the search.
stories.why_it_matters: Unlicensed mines operate across Indonesia with little safety equipment or oversight, and accidents like this are a recurring cost of an informal gold trade that many poor communities rely on.
stories.background: Indonesia has large mineral deposits, and small unlicensed mines are common, often dug by hand by local workers. These sites are prone to floods, landslides and tunnel collapses, especially in the rainy season, which runs from roughly November to March. In this case workers were inside a narrow shaft about 100 meters deep when it flooded. Indonesia's search and rescue agency is leading the operation.

stories.headline: Wall Street claws back most of a steep AI-led drop before Thanksgiving
stories.summary: U.S. stocks fell sharply early Wednesday as shares of Nvidia and other artificial-intelligence companies sold off, then recovered most of the loss by the close, though the major indexes still finished lower. Asian and European markets rose Thursday, and futures pointed to gains when U.S. trading resumes Friday.
stories.why_it_matters: A handful of AI companies now carry so much weight in the big indexes that their swings show up directly in retirement and index-fund balances. Outlets described this as the most volatile stretch for U.S. stocks in years.
stories.background: Technology and AI-related shares have been falling for several sessions as investors question how quickly heavy AI spending will turn into profits. Wednesday also brought a higher inflation reading, which reinforced expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December, and a new round of U.S. tariff announcements. Nvidia, the chipmaker at the center of the AI trade, has been especially unsettled after its chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned in mid-November and was then reinstated. U.S. markets paused for Thanksgiving on Thursday.

stories.headline: Fed's preferred inflation gauge rises to 3.8%, keeping a December rate increase in view
stories.summary: The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier, up from September, according to reports on Wednesday's release. Outlets across the spectrum said the Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise interest rates at its December meeting. Separate reports showed third-quarter economic growth revised higher and new home sales at a 10-month high.
stories.why_it_matters: Inflation near 4% means prices are still rising about twice as fast as the Fed's 2% goal, and another rate increase would push up borrowing costs on credit cards, car loans and mortgages.
stories.background: The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index is the inflation measure the Federal Reserve watches most closely when it sets interest rates. The Fed raises rates to cool spending and slow price increases, at the cost of making loans more expensive. Inflation has been climbing in recent months, and forecasters and markets had already been anticipating a December increase. Fed officials do not agree on what is driving the rise in prices, Reuters reported. The next jobs report and the Fed's December meeting are the next scheduled markers.

facts.text: The PCE price index rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier, CNBC and the New York Post reported.
The New York Post reported that the October figure was up from 3.7% in September.
The 3.8% reading matched the Dow Jones consensus forecast cited by CNBC.
The Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise interest rates next month, according to the New York Times, Fox Business and the New York Post.
Fed policymakers are at odds over the causes of high inflation, Reuters reported.
U.S. third-quarter GDP growth was revised sharply higher, Reuters and Fox Business reported.
New home sales rose 14.2% in October to a 10-month high as builders offered incentives and cut prices.
Oxford Economics said before the release that it expected a quarter-point rate increase at the December meeting.
The Fed's final 2026 policy meeting is listed for Dec. 8-9, according to Kiplinger's rundown of the Fed's schedule.
The November jobs report is scheduled for release on Friday, Dec. 4, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics calendar.

concept.explanation: A tariff is a tax a government charges on goods brought in from another country. The importer, usually a domestic company, pays it at the border, and then decides how much of the cost to absorb and how much to pass along in higher prices. Governments use tariffs to protect local industries, to raise revenue, or to pressure other countries in trade disputes, and the countries targeted often answer with tariffs of their own. For households, tariffs can show up as higher prices on imported items such as electronics, cars and clothing, and they can feed into inflation, which in turn affects whether the Federal Reserve raises or lowers interest rates.
